issuing_body: Minnesota Office of the Legislative Auditor
title: Child Care Assistance Program: Assessment of Fraud Allegations
scope: Assessment of specific allegations, not a comprehensive performance audit of CCAP or a full fraud-rate measurement.
findings: OLA did not find evidence to substantiate the allegation that Minnesota CCAP fraud was $100 million annually.

OLA believed actual CCAP fraud exceeded the $5 million to $6 million prosecutors had been able to prove at that time, but said it could not offer a reliable estimate of how much fraud existed in the program.
OLA was unable to substantiate the allegation that Minnesota CCAP fraud money was sent to a foreign country and obtained/used by a terrorist organization.
OLA found a claim that a politician interfered with a DHS investigation was misleading and concluded the case was properly handled.

money.notes: Do not publish as a validated Minnesota CCAP fraud figure.
OLA said prosecutors had been able to prove roughly $5M-$6M, while believing actual fraud was higher but not reliably estimable. Do not turn this historical range into a current fraud figure.

source_locators.summary_100m: report p.5 / PDF p.10, lines 127-144; visually confirmed on screenshot

does_not_support: The report does not establish that CCAP was free of fraud; it explicitly said proven cases likely understated the true level.
The report does not provide a reliable overall fraud rate or loss estimate.

The report's inability to substantiate the terrorism-funding allegation should not be rewritten as proof that no remitted money from any source ever reached a terrorist organization; the review addressed the specific allegation linking CCAP fraud money.
This 2019 review is historical and should not be used as a current-dollar estimate for 2026.
editorial_value: This is a strong Minnesota precedent for distinguishing a widely repeated fraud estimate from proven cases: rejecting an unsupported headline estimate does not require pretending the underlying fraud problem is zero.
